## **Structural Ambiguity**
<br>
words (or phrases and sentences) are structured **hierarchically**, not linearly<br><br>
- within a word, the same **morpheme order** can sometimes have **different** word meanings
  - <i>**un**-lockable</i> vs. <i>unlock-**able**</i><br><br>
- within a phrase or a sentence, the same **word order** can sometimes have different meanings depending on the different structures

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>[<span style="color:#CC0033">green</span> [<span style="color:blue">tea cup</span>]]</i><br><br>
<img src="../pic/0923/green2.png"width="50%">
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>[[<span style="color:#CC0033">green tea</span>] <span style="color:blue">cup<span>]</i><br><br>
<img src="../pic/0923/green1.png"width="50%">
</div>
]

---
## **Structural Ambiguity for Sentences**
<br>
sentences sometimes can be **ambiguous** depending on different hierarchical structures even when each word in the sentence has exactly **the same meaning** and they are put in **the same order**
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0923/telescope.png"width="80%">
</div>

---
## **Structural Ambiguity for Sentences**
<br>
sentences sometimes can be **ambiguous** depending on different hierarchical structures even when each word in the sentence has exactly **the same meaning** and they are put in **the same order**
<br><br><br>

--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3>(1) <i>Arthur read the book on the desk.</i></h3>
</div><br>

--

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>Arthur <span style="color:green">read the book</span> <span style="color:blue">on the desk</span></i>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>Arthur <span style="color:green">read</span> <span style="color:blue">the book on the desk</span></i>
</div>
]

<br><br>

--


<div style="text-align:center">
<h3>(2) <i>They helped the student with homework.</i></h3>
</div><br>

--

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>They <span style="color:#CC0033">helped the student</span> <span style="color:orange">with homework</span></i>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<i>They <span style="color:#CC0033">helped</span> <span style="color:orange">the student with homework</span></i>
</div>
]

## **Structure**
<br>
.pull-left[
<br><br>
- **word order** is one relevant aspect of how sentences are put together<br><br>
- but that’s **NOT** enough:<br><br>
  - <i>Arthur <span style="color:green">read</span> <span style="color:blue">the book on the table</span>.</i>
  - <i>Arthur <span style="color:green">read the book</span> <span style="color:blue">on the table</span>.</i><br><br>
- the same string of words has two different meanings<br><br>
- **hierarchical structure** is also relevant for putting words together
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/0923/doctor.jpg "width="90%">
]

class:middle, center
## **From the Ground Up**
<br><br><br><br>
### <b>large phrases and sentences</b>
### ⬆️
### <b>phrases</b>
### ⬆️
### <b>words</b>
### ⬆️
### <b>morphemes</b>

---
## **From the Ground Up**
<br>
<h3><b>large phrases and sentences</b></h3>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3>⬆️<br><br>
<b>phrases</b><br><br>
⬆️<br><br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>words</b></span><br><br>
⬆️<br><br>
<b>morphemes</b></h3>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
- like morphology, we’ll build our theory of syntax **ground-up**<br><br>
- instead of starting with morphemes, we will start with **words**<br><br>
- <u><b>first task</b></u>: figure out what **part of speech** (a.k.a syntactic category, word class) a word has<br><br>
- once we have got that down, we’ll see how they **combine** to form phrases<br><br>
- notice the parallels with Morphology, we start from each **morpheme**, then we **combine**
]

---
## **Parts of Speech**
<br>
- parts of speech (aka lexical classes) are categories we use to **classify words**:<br><br>
  - nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs...<br><br>
- they're important for **Morphology**:<br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>derivation</b></span> can change a word's part of speech<br>
  *courage* (**N**) → *en-courage* (**V**) → *en-courage-ment* (**N**)<br><br>
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>inflection</b></span> is specific to a part of speech: nouns, verbs, and adjectives all inflect differently<br>
  *walk* → *walk-ed* (-ed for **V** only) <br><br>
- they'll also be important for **Syntax**:<br><br>
  - sentences are made of words, and a word's part of speech determines its **role** in the sentence:
  - for instance, the subject of a sentence is always a noun<br>
  <span style="color:white">for instance,</span> every sentence needs a main verb...

---
## **Parts of Speech**
<br> 
- for following words, it is easy to define what they are in terms of **part of speech**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
**noun**<br>
<span style="color:green"><b>verb</b></span><br>
<span style="color:blue"><b>adjective</b></span>
]
.pull-right[
denotes a person, place, thing<br>
denotes actions<br>
adds a description to a noun
]
<br><br>

--

- so we can provide definitions of these categories, because we know the **meaning** of the word
  - table is a noun because we know it names a thing<br><br>
- can we figure out a word's part of speech without knowing what it means – just by seeing how it's used in a sentence?
  - the answer is **YES**
  - but the part of speech of a word, is determined by its **distribution**, NOT by its meaning<br><br>
- **syntactic distribution**: different categories of words appears in different positions in a sentence
- **morphological distribution**: different categories of words takes different affixes


---
.pull-left[
## **Jabberwocky**
<br>
- the words are nonsense, but the **syntax** is recognizably English<br>
- **meaning** does not tell us anything now, we have to rely on how they're being used<br><br>
- **step 1**: on the form, take your best guess at the part of speech of each **coloured** word (noun, verb, adj)<br><br>
- **step 2**: compare your answers with that of a neighbor
  - did you get the same answers?
  - what made you choose the answer you did?
]
.pull-right[
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
Twas brillig, and the <span style="color:green"><b>slithy</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>toves</b></span> <br><br>
Did <span style="color:green"><b>gyre</b></span> and gimble in the <span style="color:green"><b>wabe</b></span>; <br><br>
All mimsy were the <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span>, <br><br>
And the mome <span style="color:green"><b>raths</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>outgrabe</b></span> <br><br>
<div style="font-size:0.85em">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Lewis Carroll, <i>Jabberwocky</i> (1871)
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0923/jabberwocky.jpg" width="80%">
</div>
</div>
]

---
.pull-left[
## **Morphological Distribution**
<br>
for **morphological distribution**, we check:<br><br>
  - what morphemes does it have? 
  - are they associated with a specific part of speech?<br><br>

- consider the word <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span>:<br><br>
  - it seems to end in the plural suffix **-s**
  - what other words use plural -s?<br><br>

- we conclude <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span> is a noun (**N**)
  - because it fits the **morphological distribution** of nouns
  - it uses morphemes associated with nouns
]
.pull-right[
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
Twas brillig, and the <span style="color:green"><b>slithy</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>toves</b></span> <br><br>
Did <span style="color:green"><b>gyre</b></span> and gimble in the <span style="color:green"><b>wabe</b></span>; <br><br>
All mimsy were the <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span>, <br><br>
And the mome <span style="color:green"><b>raths</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>outgrabe</b></span> <br><br>
<div style="font-size:0.85em">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Lewis Carroll, <i>Jabberwocky</i> (1871)
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0923/jabberwocky.jpg" width="80%">
</div>
</div>
]

---
.pull-left[
## **Syntactic Distribution**
<br>
for **syntactic distribution**, we check:<br><br>
  - where does the word appear in the sentence?
  - what other words appear around it?<br><br>
  
- consider the word <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span> once more:<br><br>
  - it comes after ***the*** → *the borogoves*
  - what other words can follow ***the***?<br><br>
  
- we still conclude that <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span> is a noun (**N**)<br><br>
  - because it fits the **syntactic distribution** of nouns
  - it goes where nouns go in the sentence
]
.pull-right[
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
Twas brillig, and the <span style="color:green"><b>slithy</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>toves</b></span> <br><br>
Did <span style="color:green"><b>gyre</b></span> and gimble in the <span style="color:green"><b>wabe</b></span>; <br><br>
All mimsy were the <span style="color:green"><b>borogroves</b></span>, <br><br>
And the mome <span style="color:green"><b>raths</b></span> <span style="color:green"><b>outgrabe</b></span> <br><br>
<div style="font-size:0.85em">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Lewis Carroll, <i>Jabberwocky</i> (1871)
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0923/jabberwocky.jpg" width="80%">
</div>
</div>
]

---
## **Part of Speech**
<br>
.pull-left[
**parts of speech** aren't just random categories you have to memorize in English class<br><br>
- words of a particular part of speech tend to behave in **similar** ways:<br><br>
  - they have a similar **morphological distribution** (similar morphemes)
  - and a similar **syntactic distribution** (similar role in sentences)
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0923/pos.jpg" width="50%">
</div>
]
<br>
___

- that is, they follow a <span style="color:green"><b>pattern</b></span>
  - a <span style="color:green"><b>pattern</b></span> that forms part of our **mental grammar**
  - we pick up these <span style="color:green"><b>patterns</b></span> when acquiring our native language
  - a small child might not know what a <span style="color:blue"><b>noun</b></span> is, but they might know<br>
  *take ball*, *take toy*... but not `*` *take eat*
  - we make use of such categories like <span style="color:blue"><b>noun</b></span> and <span style="color:blue"><b>verb</b></span> before we actually know what they are
  
---
## **Parts of Speech: Replacement Test**
<br>
since these categories are part of our **mental grammar**, they give us intuitions about how a word **can** or **cannot** be used in a sentence<br><br>
- we can use these intuitions in a **replacement test** to figure out a word's part of speech:<br><br>
- let's say for the following sentence, we do not know the part of speech of **delicious**:<br><br>
  - <i>John ate a **delicious** sandwich</i>.<br><br>
- but we know the part of speech of **eat** (V) and **good** (Adj)
- we replace **delicious** with either *eat* or *good*<br><br>
   - `*` <i>John ate a(n) **eat** sandwich</i>.
   - <i>John ate a **good** sandwich</i>.<br><br>
- if the sentence after replacing is still **well-formed**, *delicious* probably has the same part of speech with the replaced word

---
## **Parts of Speech: Replacement Test**
<br>
.pull-left[
note here it might NOT **always** work!<br><br>
let's say we know the part of speech of the word **friendly** (Adj) and **good** (Adj)<br><br>
  - (a) ? <i>John ate a **friendly** sandwich</i>.
  - (b) `*` <i>John ate a(n) **eat** sandwich</i>.
  - (c) <i>John ate a **good** sandwich</i>.<br><br>

comparing the first two sentences, we know that<br><br>
  - **(a)** is syntactically well-formed, but not meaningwise proper (**semantic anomaly**)
  - but **(b)** is syntactically ill-formed (**syntactic ungrammaticality**)<br><br>
  
a famous example on the **right**
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/0923/colour.jpg" width="90%">
<br><br>
<i>Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.</i>
]

---
class: middle, center
## we will introduce following parts of speech and their **morphological** and **syntactic distributions**
<br><br>
**noun** (N): *dog*, *cat*, *teacher*<br>
**verb** (V): *eat*, *do*, *think*<br>
**adjective** (Adj): *easy*, *happy*, *wonderful*<br>
**adverb** (adv): *easily*, *happily*, *wonderfully*<br>
**determiner** (D): *the*, *my*, *a*<br>
**preposition** (P): *in*, *with*, ***to<sub>1</sub>***<br>
**conjunction** (Conj): *and*, *or*, *because*<br>
**complementiser** (C): *that*, *whether*<br>
**tense** (T): *be*, *will*, **to<sub>2</sub>**<br>

---
## **Nouns**
<br>
### **nouns** denote someone or something
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- **nouns** denote a person, place, or thing...<br><br>
-  also abstract entities, concepts, even actions
]
.pull-right[
*student*, *school*, *desk*<br><br>
*hope*, *idea*, *year*, *math fishing*
]
<br><br><br>

<span style="color:#CC0033"><b>nouns</b></span> can be further divided into<br><br>

.pull-left[
- **common nouns**<br><br>
- **proper nouns** (names)
]
.pull-right[
*girl*, *river*, *college*<br><br>
*Mary*, *Raritan*, *Rutgers*
]

---
## **Nouns**
<br>
**morphological distribution**: what affixes can a **noun** have in English?<br><br>

.pull-left[
- nouns can take plural <span style="color:green"><b>-s</b></span> or possessive <span style="color:blue"><b>'s</b></span><br><br>
- derivational morphemes that form nouns: <span style="color:orange"><b>-tion/sion</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>-ness</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>-ity</b></span>...
]
.pull-right[
cat<span style="color:green"><b>s</b></span>, dog<span style="color:green"><b>s</b></span>, Merlin<span style="color:blue"><b>'s</b></span>, students<span style="color:blue"><b>'</b></span><br><br>
happi<span style="color:orange"><b>ness</b></span>, read<span style="color:orange"><b>ing</b></span>, encourage<span style="color:orange"><b>ment</b></span>
]<br><br>

--

<span style="color:#CC0033"><b>syntactic distribution</b></span>: where do <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>nouns</b></span> appear in sentences in English?<br><br>

.pull-left[
- nouns can follow <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>determiners</b></span> like *a*, *the*, *my*<br><br>
- nouns can follow <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>adjectives</b></span><br><br>
- nouns can follow <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>prepositions</b></span><br><br>
- nouns can be <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>subjects</b></span> of sentences<br><br>
- nouns can be <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>objects</b></span> of sentences<br><br>
]
.pull-right[
<span style="color:#FF1493"><b>a</b></span> dog, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>the</b></span> cat, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>my</b></span> friend<br><br>
<span style="color:#FF1493"><b>friendly</b></span> dog, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>angry</b></span> cat, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>best</b></span> friend<br><br>
<span style="color:#FF1493"><b>at</b></span> school, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>in</b></span> line, <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>on</b></span> demand<br><br>
<span style="color:#FF1493"><b>Dogs</b></span> are humans' best friend.<br><br>
I saw <span style="color:#FF1493"><b>dogs</b></span>.
]

---
## **Pronouns**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **pronoun** takes the place of a noun
]
.pull-right[
`*` Mary had a little lamb = <span style="color:green"><b>She</b></span> had it.
]
<br><br>

- some linguists consider pronouns a **subcategory** of nouns, because they behave like nouns in many ways:<br>

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
they can be <span style="color:blue"><b>subjects</b></span>: <br><br>
they can be <span style="color:blue"><b>objects</b></span>:
</div>
]
.pull-right[
Merlin sings = <span style="color:blue"><b>He</b></span> sings.<br><br>
Did you help your mom? = Did you help <span style="color:blue"><b>her</b></span>?
]
<br><br>

- some linguists consider pronouns a **separate** part of speech, because in some ways they behave differently:<br><br>

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
they (usually) aren't modified by<br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>the</b></span> or an <span style="color:orange"><b>adjective</b></span> 
<br><br>
although: lucky <span style="color:orange"><b>you</b></span>! (idiomatic use)
</div>
]
.pull-right[
the happy student<br><br>
`*` the <span style="color:orange"><b>them</b></span><br>

`*` happy <span style="color:orange"><b>them</b></span><br><br>
]
<br>
- in this class, we'll consider them a **subcategory** of nouns, but also acknowledge their differences

---
## **Verbs**
<br>
### **verbs** can denote
<br>
.pull-left[
.pull-left[
- <span style="color:orange"><b>actions</b></span> <br><br>
- <span style="color:blue"><b>states</b></span><br><br>
- or <span style="color:green"><b>processes</b></span><br><br>
]
.pull-right[
sit, jump, fly<br><br>
be, have, know, want<br><br>
dream, feel, rest<br><br>
]
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/0923/zero.jpg" width="80%">
]
---
## **Verbs**
<br>
**morphological distribution**: what kind of morphemes can <span style="color:green"><b>English</b></span> **verbs** have?<br><br>
.pull-left[
- verbs can be conjugated for <span style="color:blue"><b>tense</b></span> & <span style="color:green"><b>subject</b></span><br><br>
- derivational morphemes can make verbs<br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>-ise</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>-ify</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>-ate</b></span>, <span style="color:orange"><b>-en</b></span>...
]
.pull-right[
I break, she break<span style="color:green"><b>s</b></span>, we <span style="color:blue"><b>broke</b></span>, we have brok<span style="color:blue"><b>en</b></span><br><br>
modern<span style="color:orange"><b>ise</b></span>, elect<span style="color:orange"><b>ify</b></span>, valid<span style="color:orange"><b>ate</b></span>, length<span style="color:orange"><b>en</b></span>
]<br><br>

--

<span style="color:#CC0033"><b>syntactic distribution</b></span>: where do <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>verbs</b></span> go in <span style="color:green"><b>English</b></span> sentences?<br><br>

.pull-left[
- verbs go <span style="color:deeppink"><b>after</b></span> the subject and <span style="color:deeppink"><b>before</b></span> object(s)<br><br>
- all sentences have at least <span style="color:deeppink"><b>one verb</b></span><br><br>
- some sentences have <span style="color:deeppink"><b>auxiliary</b></span> verbs in addition to the <span style="color:deeppink"><b>main</b></span> verb<br><br>
- <span style="color:deeppink"><b>modal</b></span> verbs are a type of auxiliary verb that express obligation, possibility, etc. 
]
.pull-right[
She <span style="color:deeppink"><b>knows</b></span> me, I <span style="color:deeppink"><b>did</b></span> it.<br><br>
I <span style="color:deeppink"><b>like</b></span> pizza. `*` I an ice cream.<br><br>
I <span style="color:deeppink"><b>am</b></span> singing. I <span style="color:deeppink"><b>have</b></span> finished.<br><br><br>
can, could, may, might, shall, should, would, must, outght to
]

---
## **Adjectives and Adverbs**
<br>
### **adjectives** and **adverbs** modify other words<br>
### providing additional description
<br>
.pull-left[
- **adjectives** modify <span style="color:deeppink"><b>nouns</b></span><br><br>
- **adverbs** modify <span style="color:green"><b>verbs</b></span><br>
  <span style="color:blue"><b>adjectives</b></span> and<br>
  other <span style="color:orange"><b>adverbs</b></span>
]
.pull-right[
<span style="color:deeppink"><b>ferocious</b></span> chihuahua<br><br>
The chihuahua barked <span style="color:green"><b>angrily</b></span>.<br>
It was <span style="color:blue"><b>extremely</b></span> aggressive.<br>
It ran <span style="color:orange"><b>very</b></span>quickly.
]
<br><br>

<span style="color:#CC0033"><b>syntactic distribution</b></span>
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- both go <span style="color:green"><b>before</b></span> the word they modify:<br><br>
- but **adverbs** can go <span style="color:green"><b>before</b></span> or <span style="color:blue"><b>after</b></span> verbs
]
.pull-right[
<span style="color:green"><b>playful</b></span> labrador, <span style="color:green"><b>very</b></span> friendly<br><br>
I <span style="color:green"><b>quickly</b></span> stopped. / I stopped <span style="color:blue"><b>quickly</b></span>.
]

---
## **Adjectives and Adverbs**
<br>
### **adjectives** and **adverbs** modify other words<br>
### providing additional description
<br>
**morphological distribution**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- many English adjectives can inflect for **comparative** and **superlative** with *-er*, *-est*<br><br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>derivational</b></span> morphemes for adjectives<br>
*-ish*, *-al*, *-ic*...<br><br>
- <span style="color:blue"><b>derivational</b></span> morpheme for adverbs: *-ly*<br><br>
  - though not all adverbs end in *-ly*
  - and some adjectives end in *-ly*, too
]
.pull-right[
nic**er**, nic**est**<br>
`*` perfect**er**, `*` perfect**est**<br><br>
book<span style="color:green"><b>ish</b></span>, person<span style="color:green"><b>al</b></span>, horrif<span style="color:green"><b>ic</b></span><br><br><br>
happi<span style="color:blue"><b>ly</b></span>, slow<span style="color:blue"><b>slowlve</b></span><br><br>
My dog runs <span style="color:orange"><b>quickly</b></span><br>
the friend<span style="color:orange"><b>ly</b></span> cat, the kind<span style="color:orange"><b>ly</b></span> man
]

---
## **Determiners**
### **determiners** help to specify a word's reference
<br>
**determiners** gather together many words you may have learned as separate categories:<br><br>
.pull-left[
- articles<br><br>
- possessive pronouns<br><br>
- demonstratives<br><br>
- interrogative determiners<br><br>
- quantifiers
]
.pull-right[
*the*, *a*<br><br>
*my*, *our*, *your*, *his*, *her*, *their*, *its*<br><br>
**this** apple, **that** barn<br><br>
**which** computer, **what** floor<br><br>
*all*, *some*, *many*
]
<br><br>
**determiners** help to specify a word's reference, what **actual** thing in the world a word refers to<br><br>
  - dog vs. **my** dog

---
## **Determiners**
<br>
**morphological distribution**<br><br>
- English determiners don't have any specific morphemes that are typical of them<br>
- in fact, they tend to be **monomorphemic**<br><br>

**syntactic distribution**<br><br>
.pull-left[
- determiners can go <span style="color:green"><b>before</b></span> a noun<br><br>
- or <span style="color:blue"><b>before</b></span> an adjective, <span style="color:blue"><b>then</b></span> a noun<br><br>
- English usually doesn't allow <span style="color:orange"><b>two</b></span> determiners in a row
]
.pull-right[
<span style="color:green"><b>the</b></span> apple, <span style="color:green"><b>my</b></span> friend<br><br>
<span style="color:blue"><b>the</b></span> red apple, <span style="color:blue"><b>my</b></span> good firend<br><br>
`*` <span style="color:orange"><b>the my</b></span> friend
]

---
## **Prepositions**
### **prepositions** indicate some relationship between a **noun**<br> and the **other words** in a sentence
<br>
  - **prepositions** can indicate:<br><br>
.pull-left[
- <span style="color:blue"><b>spatial</b></span> relationship<br><br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>grammatical</b></span> relationships<br><br>
- <span style="color:orange"><b>conceptual</b></span> relationships
]
.pull-right[
<span style="color:blue"><b>on</b></span> the table<br><br>
belong <span style="color:green"><b>to</b></span> me<br><br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>in</b></span> the morning
]<br><br>

**morphological distribution**: no specific affixes and are often **monomorphemic**<br>

**syntactic distribution**<br><br>
.pull-left[
- prepositions go **before** nouns in English<br>
(pre-position)
]
.pull-right[
**on** topic, **in** time, **with** cheese
]

---
## **Conjunctions and Complementisers**
###**conjunctions** join together two words, phrases, or clauses
<br>
  - *and*, *or*, *but*, *because*, *if*, *since*<br><br>

- <span style="color:orange"><b>coordinating conjunctions</b></span> join two words/phrases of the **same type**
  - *and*, *or*, *but*
  - <i>cats <span style="color:green"><b>and</b></span> dogs</i>, <i>coffee <span style="color:green"><b>or</b></span> tea</i>
  - **syntactic distribution**: between the two elements being joined<br><br>

- <span style="color:blue"><b>subordinating conjunctions</b></span> are used to insert one sentence (subordinate clause) into another sentence (main clause) and they are also called <span style="color:blue"><b>complementisers</b></span>
  - *because*, *that*, *if*, *since*, *whether* 
  - <i>I went to bed <span style="color:blue"><b>because</b></span> I was tired</i>. / <i><span style="color:blue"><b>If</b></span> you study, you will succeed</i>.
  - **syntactic distribution**: before the subordinate clause being inserted

---
## **Tense and Aspect**
<br>
### **tense** refers to when an action occurs<br> whether it happens in the <span style="color:blue"><b>past</b></span>, <span style="color:green"><b>present</b></span> or <span style="color:orange"><b>future</b></span>
.pull-left[
- tells **WHEN** the action occurs
- <span style="color:blue"><b>past</b></span> tense: *She walk<span style="color:blue"><b>ed</b></span> to school*.
- <span style="color:green"><b>present</b></span> tense: *She walk<span style="color:green"><b>s</b></span> to school*
- <span style="color:orange"><b>future</b></span> tense: *She <span style="color:orange"><b>will</b></span> walk to school.*
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:right">
<br>
<span style="color:blue"><b>PST</b></span><br>
<span style="color:green"><b>PRES</b></span><br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>FUT</b></span>
</div>
]
<br><br>
<h3><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>aspect</b></span> refers to the state of the action<br> whether it is <span style="color:blue"><b>ongoing</b></span>, <span style="color:green"><b>completed</b></span> or <span style="color:orange"><b>habitual</b></span></h3>
.pull-left[
- tells **HOW** the action unfolds
- <span style="color:blue"><b>progressive</b></span> aspect: *She <span style="color:blue"><b>is</b></span> walk<span style="color:blue"><b>ing</b></span> to school.*
- <span style="color:green"><b>perfective</b></span> aspect: *She <span style="color:green"><b>has</b></span> walked to school.*
- <span style="color:orange"><b>habitual</b></span> aspect: *She walk<span style="color:orange"><b>s</b> </span><span style="color:orange"><b>every day</b></span>.*
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:right">
<br>
<span style="color:blue"><b>PROG</b></span><br>
<span style="color:green"><b>PERF</b></span><br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>HAB</b></span>
</div>
]

---
## **Tense and Aspect**
<br>
### **tense** refers to when an action occurs<br> whether it happens in the <span style="color:blue"><b>past</b></span>, <span style="color:green"><b>present</b></span> or <span style="color:orange"><b>future</b></span>
.pull-left[
- tells **WHEN** the action occurs
- <span style="color:blue"><b>past</b></span> tense: *She walk<span style="color:blue"><b>ed</b></span> to school*.
- <span style="color:green"><b>present</b></span> tense: *She walk<span style="color:green"><b>s</b></span> to school*
- <span style="color:orange"><b>future</b></span> tense: *She <span style="color:orange"><b>will</b></span> walk to school.*
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:right">
<br>
<span style="color:blue"><b>PST</b></span><br>
<span style="color:green"><b>PRES</b></span><br>
<span style="color:orange"><b>FUT</b></span>
</div>
]
<br><br><br><br>
.pull-left[
<b>auxiliaries</b><br><br>
<b>modals</b><br><br><br>
<b>non-finite tense marker</b>
]
.pull-right[
*has/have/had*, *am/is/are/was/were*, *do/does/did*<br><br>
*will*, *would*, *shall*, *should*,<br>
*can*, *could*, *may*, *might*, *must*<br><br>
*to*
]

### Nootka, Wakashan 
<br>
.pull-left[
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; text-align:left;">
  <tr>
    <td>(a)</td>
    <td>mamu:k<span style="color:blue">-ma</span></td>
    <td>qu:ʔas<span style="color:green">-ʔi</span></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <td>working<span style="color:blue">-PRES</span></td>
    <td>man<span style="color:green">-DEF</span></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <td>'The man is working.'</td>
    <td></td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr><td><span style="color:white">-</span></td></tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>(b)</td>
    <td>qu:ʔas<span style="color:blue">-ma</span></td>
    <td>mamu:k<span style="color:green">-ʔi</span></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <td>man<span style="color:blue">-PRES</span></td>
    <td>walking<span style="color:green">-DEF</span></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td></td>
    <td>'The working one is a man.'</td>
    <td></td>
  </tr>
</table>
]
.pull-right[
- <span style="color:blue"><b>PRES</b></span> = present tense<br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>DEF</b></span> = definite<br><br>

1. What’s the **noun** in (a)? What’s the <span style="color:orange"><b>verb</b></span>?<br><br>

]

<h3>in both sentences:</h3>
<br>
- the first part is the <span style="color:orange"><b>verb</b></span><br>

-  the second part is the **noun**<br>
  - indicated by the <span style="color:green"><b>definite</b></span> morpheme <span style="color:green">-ʔi</span>


---
## **Open and Closed Classes**
<br>
- parts of speech can be divided into **open** and **closed classes**<br><br>
- **open class**: words have more of a **lexical** meaning<br><br>
  - typical dictionary definition
  - it's fairly easy to *borrow* or *coin* new words in these categories
  - nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs<br><br>
- **closed class**: words have more of a **grammatical** meaning<br><br>
  - it's less common, but not impossible, to borrow or coin new words in these categories
  - determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, complementisers, tense

---

2. John went to New York yesterday.<br><br><br>
3. A cat is under the table.<br><br><br>
4. Her dad was fixing a car.

---
## **Summary**
<br>
- **parts of speech** are categories of words that tend to behave in similar ways:<br><br>
  - noun, verb, adjective, adverb, determiner, preposition, conjunction, complementiser, tense<br><br>
- we often learn them in school by definition<br><br>
- but we figure them out here based on **context**, by considering their:<br><br>
  - **morphological distribution** – what kinds of morphemes they have.
  - **syntactic distribution** – where they tend to appear in the sentence<br><br>
- by examining their **distribution**, we can notice patterns in the way certain types of words behave<br><br>
- and this will be fundamental to our understanding of **syntax**, as we start putting words together to form **sentences**
